p1: Little Bighorn (1876): Crazy Horse and Sitting Bull led 2,000+ warriors → annihilated Custer's 7th Cavalry (268 dead) → largest Native military victory of the Plains Wars
p2: Aftermath: Army flooded Plains with reinforcements → Sitting Bull fled to Canada → Crazy Horse surrendered and was killed in custody (1877) → Black Hills seized in violation of Fort Laramie Treaty
p3: Significance: briefly raised morale but accelerated federal military response → proved Natives could win battles but could not win the war → by 1877 major armed resistance effectively ended

front: What was the impact of the Homestead Act and railroad on Natives?
p1: Homestead Act (1862): granted settlers 160-acre plots on Native lands → 270 million acres distributed by 1900 → directly displaced tribes from ancestral territories
p2: Transcontinental railroad (1869): opened Plains to mass settlement → destroyed buffalo migration routes → military used railroad to rapidly transport troops to suppress resistance
p3: Impact: Plains tribes lost economic base (buffalo) and territorial integrity within a decade → forced onto increasingly marginal reservation lands → set conditions for Dawes Act dispossession

front: What was the significance of the buffalo extermination?
p1: Buffalo central to Plains tribes — food, clothing, shelter, spiritual practice. 30 million buffalo in 1800 → fewer than 1,000 by 1889
p2: Deliberate policy: Army encouraged hunters. General Sheridan: 'destroying the buffalo destroyed Native independence' → Army killed 10 million buffalo 1865-83
p3: Without buffalo, Plains tribes faced starvation → forced dependency on government rations → undermined economic and cultural autonomy

front: What was the Long Walk of the Navajo (1864–66)?
p1: Kit Carson destroyed Navajo crops, orchards and livestock — forced surrender. 8,000–9,000 Navajo forced on 300-mile march to Bosque Redondo reservation, New Mexico — winter conditions. Thousands died from starvation, exposure and disease en route.
p2: Bosque Redondo: barren, alkaline soil, contaminated water — crops failed repeatedly. 3,000 Navajo died in four years from disease and starvation. Government rationing inadequate, BIA agents corrupt.
p3: Treaty of 1868: Navajo allowed to return to ancestral lands — one of the few treaty victories of the period. Reservation expanded 4 million

front: What was the significance of Crazy Horse and Sitting Bull?
p1: Sitting Bull (Hunkpapa Lakota): spiritual leader → refused to sign treaties → led resistance against US expansion → key figure at Little Bighorn (1876)
p2: Crazy Horse (Oglala Lakota): greatest military tactician → never signed a treaty → led warriors at Little Bighorn → surrendered 1877 → killed in custody by US soldiers
p3: Significance: demonstrated united resistance could defeat US Army → inspired Native resistance movements → BUT US Army ultimately overwhelmed all military resistance by 1877

front: What was the significance of the Black Hills to the Sioux?
p1: Black Hills (Paha Sapa): sacred to Sioux → Treaty of Fort Laramie (1868): guaranteed Black Hills 'in perpetuity' → gold discovered 1874 → Sioux refused to sell.
p2: 1877: Black Hills seized in violation of treaty → government threatened to stop rations → Mount Rushmore (1927-41) carved into sacred land without consent.
p3: US v Sioux Nation (1980): $106 million awarded → Sioux refused → fund grown to $600m+ by 1992, still unclaimed.

front: What was the Indian Appropriations Act (1871)?
p1: Indian Appropriations Act (1871): tribes no longer recognised as independent nations → ended treaty-making → tribes became 'wards of state' → no legal standing to challenge dispossession
p2: Practical consequences: BIA agents took increasing control of reservation life → allotment of individual plots replaced communal land → tribes lost ability to govern themselves
p3: Significance: transformed the legal relationship between tribes and federal government → enabled Dawes Act (1887) and subsequent dispossession without treaty obligations

front: What was the Dawes Severalty Act (1887) and how did it work?
p1: Dawes Severalty Act (1887): divided communal tribal lands into 160-acre allotments. 'Surplus' land sold to white settlers. Curtis Act (1898) extended to Five Civilised Tribes
p2: Land loss: Native-owned land fell from 156 million acres (1887) to 78 million by 1900 → most allotments lost through sale, fraud or inheritance division
p3: Cultural impact: undermined communal structure → matriarchal tribes lost power as land given to male heads of families → most failed to farm — sold for survival

front: What was the cultural and gendered impact of the Dawes Act?
p1: Imposed male-headed family ownership onto matriarchal tribes → Iroquois and Cherokee women traditionally managed land → Dawes Act stripped this role
p2: Allotment scattered families across individual plots → broke up spatial concentration of tribes → undermined communal ceremonies, governance and economic co-operation
p3: Land sold to speculators: most allotted land poor quality → arid, infertile, unsuitable for farming → most sold allotments → left destitute

front: What were the key court cases and laws that destroyed Native sovereignty after 1883?
p1: Crow Dog Case (1883): tribal criminal jurisdiction recognised → BUT Congress responded with Major Crimes Act (1885): federal jurisdiction over 7 serious crimes on reservations
p2: Cherokee Nation v Hitchcock (1902): Congress had plenary authority over Native affairs → Lone Wolf v Hitchcock (1903): Congress could unilaterally revoke treaties — eliminated legal protection
p3: Dead Indian Act (1902): allowed sale of inherited allotment land — accelerated dispossession. Together these rulings closed all legal avenues for Native resistance

front: What was the Ghost Dance Movement (1889) and what did it represent?
p1: Ghost Dance Movement (1889): founded by Wovoka (Paiute prophet) → combined traditional beliefs with hope of driving away white settlers and restoring Native lands
p2: Federal government alarmed: mass gatherings seen as military threat → Sitting Bull arrested and killed by Indian police (December 1890) → 7th Cavalry surrounded Lakota at Wounded Knee Creek
p3: Significance: end of armed Plains Indian resistance → Ghost Dance suppressed — last major cultural resistance movement of the period → Wounded Knee became enduring symbol of Native suffering

front: What was the Carlisle boarding school system?
p1: Carlisle Indian Industrial School (Pennsylvania, 1879): Colonel Richard Pratt — 'kill the Indian, save the man' → children forbidden to speak languages, practice traditions or wear traditional clothing
p2: Scale: 100,000+ children forced in by early 1900s → death rates 30-50% from neglect, abuse and malnutrition → Navajo students: 13¢/day for lunch vs recommended 50¢
p3: Long-term trauma: graduates returned alienated from both worlds → boarding schools weakened matriarchal structures → cultural trauma passed through generations → contributed to high alcoholism and suicide rates on reservations

front: What was the role of Helen Hunt Jackson and the Indian Rights Association?
p1: A Century of Dishonour (1881): Helen Hunt Jackson documented US government's broken treaties and massacres → sent to every member of Congress → direct influence on reform debates
p2: Indian Rights Association (IRA, 1882): white reformers advocated for Native education and citizenship → pushed for Dawes Act as path to 'civilisation' → well-intentioned but imposed white assimilationist values
p3: Limits: Century of Dishonour raised awareness but led to Dawes Act — which caused further land loss → reformers prioritised assimilation over sovereignty → undermined cultural preservation

front: What was the impact of reservations on Native Americans? (positives)
p1: Reservations allowed tribal life to continue in limited forms — cultural identity and community sustained. Better healthcare than nomadic lifestyle, albeit very limited. Some gained jobs as interpreters, scouts or Indian Agency workers.
p2: Navajo success: reservation expanded from 4 million to 10.5 million acres. Sheep and goats: 15,000 → 1.7 million. Population grew from 8,000 (1868) to 22,000 by 1900 — only major demographic recovery.
p3: Territorial base: reservations provided defined land holdings that could be defended legally → basis for later sovereignty arguments — though severely limited by BIA paternalism

front: What was the impact of reservations on Native Americans? (limitations)
p1: Land infertile, difficult to farm → many dependent on insufficient government rations → late 1880s: government cut meat subsidies to Sioux — starvation → by 1900 only 100,000 of 240,000 Plains Indians remained.
p2: BIA corrupt: agents stole rations, manipulated accounts → 1871 Act abolished tribal sovereignty → no legal recourse → reservations became 'ghettos in the wilderness'.
p3: Cultural destruction: hunting and leadership roles removed → matriarchal tribes: women lost status as Dawes Act gave land to male heads of families → Sun Dance, Ghost Dance suppressed.

front: What were the positive effects of assimilation policies on Native Americans?
p1: Boarding schools: vocational training — domestic skills for girls, trade skills for boys → Carlisle Indian Industrial School (1879): Colonel Pratt's model → some graduates gained employment in white economy
p2: Dawes Act (1887): some Native Americans used 160-acre allotments successfully → access to agricultural markets → Five Civilised Tribes had established schools, newspapers and governments before Curtis Act
p3: Limited integration: some Native Americans adapted to white economic structures → educated elite emerged (doctors, lawyers) → BUT success was exception not rule — most allotments lost or unworkable

front: What were the damaging effects of assimilation policies on Native Americans?
p1: Cultural destruction: Sun Dance banned, buffalo hunting forbidden → boarding schools: 100,000+ children by early 1900s → forbidden to speak languages or practice traditions → death rates 30-50%
p2: Land loss: Dawes Act → Native-owned land dropped from 156 million acres (1881) to 78 million acres by 1900 → allotments often poor quality → most sold or lost within a generation
p3: Social consequences: graduates returned alienated from both worlds → matriarchal structures weakened (land given to male heads of families) → economic dependency on government rations

front: What was the Wounded Knee Massacre (1890) and why was it significant?
p1: Ghost Dance (1889): Wovoka — 5 days of dance to reconnect with ancestors and restore lost lands → spread rapidly across Plains → US Army alarmed by mass gatherings
p2: December 1890: 7th Cavalry surrounded Lakota at Wounded Knee Creek → shot fired, possibly accidentally → cavalry opened fire → 250+ Lakota killed — men, women and children
p3: Significance: end of armed Plains Indian resistance → Ghost Dance suppressed → last major cultural and military resistance movement of the 19th century → confirmed US military dominance

front: What was the role of the Five Civilised Tribes and Sequoyah Convention?
p1: Five Civilised Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole): written constitutions, elected governments, mixed economy → occupied Indian Territory (Oklahoma) → exempt from Dawes Act allotment until Curtis Act (1898).
p2: Curtis Act (1898): destroyed Five Civilised Tribes' governments — allotment imposed without consent → Muskogee/Sequoyah Convention (1905): tribal leaders proposed all-Native state of Sequoyah — own governor and Congress representatives — direct democratic response to dispossession
p3: Congress rejected Sequoyah → Oklahoma created 1907, merging Indian Territory with Oklahoma Territory → showed Native Americans could govern successfully on own terms

front: What was the role of BIA corruption and paternalism?
p1: BIA (Bureau of Indian Affairs): tribes became 'wards of state' after Indian Appropriations Act (1871) → no legal standing → BIA agents controlled access to schools, healthcare, employment and housing
p2: Corruption: agents took commissions from contractors → misallocated rations → late 1880s: government cut meat subsidies to Sioux reservations → starvation → Dawes allotment poorly administered
p3: Paternalism: BIA assumed Native Americans incapable of self-governance → decisions made without tribal consultation → reinforced dependency → reservation conditions deteriorated throughout the period

front: What was the significance of the Society of American Indians (SAI, 1911)?
p1: Society of American Indians (SAI, 1911): first national Native American rights organisation led by educated Native Americans → advocated for citizenship, land reform and end of BIA
p2: Significant figures: Carlos Montezuma demanded abolition of BIA → Gertrude Bonnin (Zitkala-Sa) documented boarding school trauma → Arthur Parker promoted Native history and pride
p3: Limitations: divisions between assimilationist and sovereignty factions → split over peyote use → collapsed by 1920s → did not survive the interwar period but established pan-tribal advocacy model

front: What was the impact of WWI service on Native Americans?
p1: WWI: 12,000 Native Americans served (some estimates 17,000) → many not yet citizens → demonstrated loyalty to nation that denied them rights → used as scouts and code communicators
p2: Indian Citizenship Act (1924): citizenship granted to all Native Americans partly in recognition of WWI service → BUT many states still barred Native Americans from voting through poll taxes and tests
p3: Limited gains: citizenship did not bring equality → BIA retained control → reservations remained impoverished → citizenship without rights — a largely symbolic gesture

front: What was the significance of the Indian Citizenship Act (1924)?
p1: Indian Citizenship Act (1924): citizenship granted to all Native Americans → BUT two-thirds already citizens through Dawes Act allotments, military service or individual treaties
p2: Practical limits: many states barred Native Americans from voting through state-level literacy tests and poll taxes → Arizona did not recognise Native voting rights until forced by courts in late 1940s
p3: Significance: formal recognition of Native Americans as full citizens → BUT BIA retained paternalistic control → citizenship did not translate to political power or economic improvement

front: What was the significance of AIDA, the Leavitt Bill and Meriam Report?
p1: AIDA (1923): Collier founded → blocked Leavitt Bill (1926) which sought to ban traditional Pueblo dances — significant cultural preservation victory
p2: Meriam Report (1928): documented appalling poverty, disease and death rates on reservations — triggered federal acknowledgement that assimilation had failed
p3: AAIA (1922): opposed sale of Native lands — aligned with campaigns against termination in 1950s-60s. Non-Native groups divided: IRA promoted assimilation; AIDA/AAIA supported preservation

front: What was the significance of John Collier and the AIDA?
p1: John Collier: lived among Pueblo communities in New Mexico 1920s → founded AIDA (1923) → blocked Leavitt Bill (1926): 'Dance Order' seeking to ban Pueblo religious dances.
p2: Commissioner for Indian Affairs (1933-45): drove Indian Reorganization Act (1934) → ended allotment, encouraged tribal self-governance, protected cultural practices.
p3: Limits: policies based on Pueblo and Navajo experience → didn't suit all tribes → Navajo rejected IRA due to livestock reduction → 25% of tribes rejected IRA outright.

front: What did the Indian Reorganization Act (Wheeler-Howard Act, 1934) do?
p1: Wheeler-Howard Act (1934): halted Dawes Act allotment → recovered unallocated land → restored 4 million of 90 million acres lost → established tribal constitutions and elected tribal councils
p2: Economic improvements: CCC-ID employed 85,000 Native Americans 1933-42 → planted 25 million trees, built 6,500 miles of road
p3: Significance: decisive ideological shift from assimilation to self-determination → reversed 50 years of federal policy → BUT 82% of Native Americans still below poverty line by 1940

front: What were the limitations of the Indian Reorganization Act (1934)?
p1: Collier's approach failed to account for Native diversity → policies based on Pueblo and Navajo experience → 25% of tribes rejected IRA outright → presumed all wanted same form of self-determination.
p2: Navajo rejected IRA: livestock reduction 1933-36 → 150,000 sheep, goats and horses killed → sheep were women's property in matrilineal Navajo society → economic and cultural devastation.
p3: Chronic underfunding: 82% below poverty line by 1940 → only $2 million annually for land buyback → boarding schools continued → paternalism did not end with Collier.

front: What was the role of the IECW/CCC-ID in the New Deal?
p1: IECW/CCC-ID: New Deal employment for Native Americans → 85,000 employed 1933-42 → planted 25 million trees, built 6,500 miles of road → surplus army clothing distributed
p2: Cultural: Indian Arts and Crafts Board (1935): revived Native arts as economic ventures → cultural education funding up 65% (1935-40) → tribal councils reinstated → ceremonial dance bans overturned
p3: Limits: Navajo students 13¢/day for lunch vs recommended 50¢ → only $2 million annually to buy back lost land

front: What was the Navajo livestock reduction and why did it matter?
p1: Navajo sheep and goat herds: 1.7 million — central to economy, culture and identity → Collier and federal scientists believed overgrazing destroying Navajo land → government ordered livestock reduction 1933-36
p2: Navajo experience: sheep were wealth, spiritual connection and family heritage → their destruction was economic and cultural devastation → women especially affected — Navajo society matrilineal, sheep traditionally women's property
p3: Consequence: Navajo rejected IRA (1934) outright → tribe Collier most wanted to help refused because of livestock reduction

front: What was the role of the NCAI and Indian Claims Commission?
p1: NCAI (National Congress of American Indians, 1944): first large-scale pan-tribal advocacy organisation → opposed termination policy → lobbied Congress for treaty rights
p2: Indian Claims Commission (1946): established to compensate for land taken → awarded cash, not land return → by 1950s, $1.3 billion in claims filed → slow process, many denied
p3: Limitations: NCAI focused on legal channels — too slow and moderate to address immediate poverty → ICC offered money not land → termination proceeded despite NCAI opposition

front: What was the significance of the Navajo Code Talkers and Ira Hayes?
p1: Navajo Code Talkers: 400-500 Navajo marines used Navajo language as unbreakable military code → Major Howard Connor: 'Were it not for the Navajos, the Marines would never have taken Iwo Jima'
p2: Native Americans in WWII: over 25,000 served → fought for democracy abroad while denied rights at home → Japanese American internment camps built on Native land
p3: Limited post-war gains: veterans returned to reservations still facing poverty, BIA control and disenfranchisement → GI Bill benefits difficult to access on reservations → Truman's civil rights focus did not extend to Natives

front: What was the impact of Japanese internment on Native lands?
p1: WWII Japanese internment: Poston internment camp built on Colorado River Indian Reservation without tribal consent → 17,000 Japanese Americans housed on Navajo and Mohave lands.
p2: Harrison v Laveen (1948): Arizona recognised Native voting rights — last state to do so → 44,000 Native Americans had served in WWII, strengthening citizenship claims.
p3: BUT Termination Policy (1953) immediately reversed post-war progress → 109 tribes terminated → economic base destroyed.

front: What was the Termination Policy (1953) and what were its consequences?
p1: Termination Policy (1953-68): ended federal recognition for 109 tribes → sold their lands, terminated healthcare, education and legal protections → Menominee (Wisconsin) and Klamath (Oregon) worst affected.
p2: Consequences: extreme poverty → terminated tribes lost all federal support → many lost land to private developers → Menominee hospital closed → malnutrition rates soared.
p3: NCAI lobbied against termination → Nixon formally ended it (1970) → Menominee Restoration Act (1973): first tribe restored → showed termination had been catastrophic failure.

front: What was the Indian Relocation Act (1956) and what were its consequences?
p1: Indian Relocation Act (1956): BIA provided one-way bus tickets to cities — Chicago, Los Angeles, Denver → promised jobs and housing → by 1970: 40% of Native Americans living in cities.
p2: Reality: urban poverty often replaced reservation poverty → housing substandard → jobs scarce → cultural isolation — no tribal community or BIA follow-up.
p3: AIM (1968) founded in Minneapolis by urban Natives who had experienced relocation → direct line from Relocation Act to AIM militancy.

front: What was the significance of the NIYC (1961) and the fish-ins?
p1: NIYC (National Indian Youth Council, 1961): first militant pan-tribal youth organisation → fish-ins in Pacific Northwest to assert treaty fishing rights — deliberately modelled on Black civil rights sit-ins
p2: Fish-ins: Native Americans exercised treaty rights in defiance of state fishing laws → arrested → publicised in national media → demonstrated treaty rights could be asserted through civil disobedience
p3: Significance: shift from NCAI's moderate legal approach → direct action → influenced AIM's later tactics → demonstrated treaty rights were enforceable through protest

front: What was the impact of reservation poverty as a structural condition?
p1: 1960s: per capita income on reservations half the national average → unemployment on many reservations 40-80% → infant mortality three times higher than national average
p2: BIA dependence: tribes had little control over their own resources → federal funding inadequate and subject to political winds → termination (1953) devastated already-weak tribal economies
p3: Urban relocation: Indian Relocation Act (1956) → BIA offered one-way tickets to cities → without community support many fell into poverty in urban ghettos → relocation failed to solve reservation poverty

front: What was Red Power and how did it differ from earlier activism?
p1: Red Power: militant movement for Native rights → emerged late 1960s, inspired by Black Power → rejected assimilation, demanded treaty rights and sovereignty
p2: AIM (1968): founded Minneapolis → urban Natives — patrol police to document brutality → Alcatraz occupation (1969-71): 'Indians of All Tribes' occupied for 19 months demanding unused land return
p3: Different from earlier: NCAI used legal channels, NIYC used civil disobedience — Red Power added armed confrontation (Wounded Knee 1973, Trail of Broken Treaties 1972) and media spectacle

front: How did Black Power influence Red Power?
p1: Direct influence: AIM (1968) modelled on Black Panthers — red berets, leather jackets → 'Red Power' directly inspired by 'Black Power'
p2: Limits: Native activism pre-dated Black Power → NIYC (1961) fish-ins already underway → NCAI (1944) established → Great Society and War on Poverty laid groundwork independently
p3: Alcatraz (1969): 10,000 Natives visited — media impact mirrored Panthers' → BUT sovereignty claims were specifically about land and treaty rights — not civil rights integration

front: What was the significance of AIM's founding (1968) and early actions?
p1: AIM (1968): founded Minneapolis → urban Natives patrolled police to document brutality → demanded sovereignty and treaty rights through direct action
p2: LBJ's 'Forgotten Americans' speech (1968). Dee Brown's Bury My Heart at Wounded Knee (1970) raised public awareness. Nixon returned Taos Blue Lake to Pueblo (1970)
p3: Indian Civil Rights Act (1968): extended constitutional protections to Natives under tribal governments — sovereignty concerns remained

front: What was the significance of the Alcatraz Occupation (1969–71)?
p1: Led by Richard Oakes (Mohawk) and 'Indians of All Tribes' → occupied Alcatraz November 1969 → claimed 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty gave Natives right to unused federal land
p2: 19-month occupation → 10,000 Natives visited → generated massive national media coverage and public sympathy → demanded federal land for Native university, cultural centre and museum
p3: Limits: Richard Oakes' daughter died in fall during occupation (1970) → Oakes left → occupation ended 1971 without policy changes → BUT sparked Red Power movement nationally

front: What was the significance of the Wounded Knee Occupation (1973)?
p1: 71-day standoff at Wounded Knee, South Dakota (1973): AIM members and Oglala Lakota occupied the town
p2: Pine Ridge: AIM arrived to support Oglala Lakota residents against corrupt tribal chairman Dick Wilson and his 'Guardians of the Oglala Nation' (GOONs) — accused of intimidation and murder → 71-day standoff, federal marshals surrounded the village → 2 AIM members killed, hundreds arrested
p3: Significance: brought international attention to Native rights — compared by some to Selma → exposed BIA corruption → BUT 600+ arrested, leaders tried for years → movement fragmented afterwards

front: What was the significance of the Trail of Broken Treaties (1972)?
p1: November 1972: cross-country caravan of multiple tribes drove to Washington DC before presidential election → demanded restoration of Native sovereignty and treaty-making rights → occupied BIA headquarters for several days.
p2: 20-point manifesto: treaty enforcement, restoration of tribal land base, abolition of BIA, new treaty relationships → Nixon administration negotiated rather than use force — election timing made confrontation politically costly
p3: Significance: most effective pan-tribal organisation in Red Power era → BIA occupation symbolically powerful → led directly to Wounded Knee (1973)

front: What was the significance of Nixon ending termination and the Self-Determination Act?
p1: Nixon (1970): formally ended termination policy — acknowledged it had been wrong. Federal government began restoring recognition to terminated tribes. Menominee restored 1973.
p2: Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (1975): tribes allowed to administer their own federal programmes → BIA contracts transferred to tribal control → 200+ tribes administering own services by late 1970s
p3: AIRFA (1978): American Indian Religious Freedom Act → protected traditional practices → ICWA (1978): tribes gained authority over child welfare → shift from assimilation to self-determination complete

front: What was the significance of NARF and Oneida v Oneida (1974)?
p1: NARF (Native American Rights Fund, 1970): provided legal representation for tribes → handled landmark cases on sovereignty, water rights, religious freedom and treaty rights
p2: Oneida v Oneida (1974): tribes could sue states for land taken in violation of treaties → opened door to land claims across eastern US → multiple tribes pursued cases
p3: US v Sioux Nation (1980): Supreme Court awarded $106 million for Black Hills taken in violation of Fort Laramie Treaty → Sioux refused — demanded land return → money sat in trust unclaimed

front: What was the significance of AIRFA and the Indian Child Welfare Act?
p1: AIRFA (American Indian Religious Freedom Act, 1978): protected right to practice traditional religions → reversed decades of ceremony bans — Sun Dance, Ghost Dance suppressed since 1880s → allowed access to sacred sites.
p2: ICWA (Indian Child Welfare Act, 1978): prevented removal of Native children to non-Native homes → tribal authority over child welfare → addressed systematic removal since boarding school era.
p3: AIRFA had no enforcement mechanism → 70% of Native religious leaders still struggled accessing sacred sites by 1992 → Graves Protection Act (1990) returned 10,000 sacred items.

front: What was the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act and position by 1992?
p1: Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (1988): tribes could establish casinos → 150 Native American-run casinos by early 1990s generating over $1 billion annually
p2: Languages Act (1990): 100+ programmes active. Charrier v Bell (1986): burial sites protected. Indian Education Act (1972): tribal education control. Columbus 500th (1992): widespread protests
p3: Continuing challenges: 25% below poverty line → less than 60% graduated high school → 50% registered to vote → federal funding inadequate

front: What was the significance of US v Sioux Nation (1980) and NARF (1970)?
p1: US v Sioux Nation (1980): Black Hills illegally seized in 1877 → $106 million awarded → Sioux refused: 'The Black Hills are not for sale'
p2: Oneida v Oneida (1974): Oneida Nation could sue for land claims under federal treaties → precedent for dozens of tribal land claims
p3: Fisher v Montana (1976): tribes decide on adoptions → Bryan v Itasca (1976): states cannot tax reservations → Seminole v Butterworth (1982): tribal casino sovereignty

front: What was the right to land for Native Americans by 1992?
p1: Indian Claims Commission (1946): awarded $800 million in compensation — but only money, not land → Sioux refused $106 million for Black Hills: 'not for sale' → fund grown to $600m+ unclaimed.
p2: NARF secured legal victories: Oneida (1974), Fisher (1976), Bryan (1976) → some land returned through settlements → BUT 30% of Native Americans still on reservations facing land loss.
p3: Gaming Act (1988): economic use of reservation land → 150 casinos generating $1 billion+ → but land sovereignty still limited by federal oversight and inconsistent legal protections.

front: What was the right to self-determination for Native Americans by 1992?
p1: Indian Self-Determination Act (1975): 200+ tribes administering own federal programmes → tribal courts recognised → AIM had forced political visibility through Alcatraz (1969) and Wounded Knee (1973).
p2: Bryan v Itasca (1976): states cannot tax reservations → tribal sovereignty affirmed in court → BUT 60% of tribes still economically reliant on federal funding → sovereignty practically limited.
p3: All citizens since 1924 → voting in all states since Laveen (1948) → BUT only 50% registered to vote in 1992 → voter turnout low → political influence marginal.

front: What were cultural and religious freedoms for Native Americans by 1992?
p1: AIRFA (1978): protected traditional practices — but 70% of Native religious leaders reported ongoing struggles accessing sacred lands by 1992
p2: Indian Arts and Crafts Act (1990): prevented exploitation by non-Native sellers → multi-million-dollar industry. Languages Act (1990): 100+ programmes. NAGPRA (1990): 10,000+ items returned
p3: Over 100 Native language programmes active → preserving languages at risk of disappearing. But enforcement of AIRFA remained weak — sacred sites still inaccessible

front: What were the broader political and economic rights of Native Americans by 1992?
p1: U.S. citizens since 1924, voting in all states since Laveen (1948) → but only 50% registered to vote → voter turnout low → political influence marginal at federal level.
p2: Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (1988): 150 casinos generating $1 billion+ annually → first major economic opportunity → BUT 25% of Native families still below poverty line → 60% reliant on federal assistance.
p3: Education: less than 60% graduated high school → only 10% held college degrees → life expectancy 5-10 years below national average.

front: What was coverture?
p1: Legal doctrine: married woman's identity subsumed into husband's → could not own property, sign contracts or keep wages → no legal recourse against abusive husbands → divorce deeply stigmatised.
p2: Effects: husbands controlled all marital property and earnings → women could not run businesses, take loans or appear in court independently → married women had no independent legal existence.
p3: Erosion: Married Women's Property Acts — state reforms from 1870s. Equal Credit Opportunity Act (1974): women's right to independent credit. ERA failed (1982) → no constitutional end to all coverture-based discrimination.

front: What was the cult of domesticity?
p1: Separate spheres: men in public sphere — politics, business, law → women confined to private sphere — home, children, moral guardianship → women expected to be pious, pure, domestic, submissive. Some women formed 'Boston Marriages' instead — supportive partnerships outside this norm.
p2: Consequences: women's campaigns had to be framed as 'moral' concerns to be acceptable → temperance, abolitionism, settlement houses → 1 in 5 women died in childbirth
p3: Persistence: Dr Spock's Baby and Child Care (1946) — 23 million copies → reinforced 1950s housewife ideal → Friedan's Feminine Mystique (1963) named the ideology's psychological damage

front: What were the political rights of women in 1865?
p1: No vote at any level → Seneca Falls (1848) had demanded suffrage but gains minimal → NWSA and AWSA not yet formed (both 1869) → 15th Amendment (1870) would give Black men the vote but exclude women entirely.
p2: No right to sit on juries, hold public office or stand for election → Minor v Happersett (1875) would confirm citizenship did not guarantee vote.
p3: Some women beginning to organise: Susan B. Anthony and Elizabeth Cady Stanton campaigning → WCTU formed 1874 → Wyoming Territory granted female suffrage 1869.

front: What was the social position of women in 1865?
p1: Coverture: husband controlled all property, contracts and wages → average 5-7 children → 1 in 5 died in childbirth → only 3% attended college vs 25% of men.
p2: Cult of domesticity: women confined to 'private sphere' — home, family, religion → any paid work seen as failure of husband's duty → immigrant women 70 hours/week in sweatshops.
p3: Comstock Laws (1873) would criminalise contraceptive information → no reproductive rights → divorce almost impossible → domestic violence not recognised as crime.

front: What was the economic position of women in 1865?
p1: 15% employed outside home → 17% in industrial jobs at half male wages → 40% of Black women in South in domestic service — no legal protection or union membership.
p2: AFL-CIO not yet formed but predecessor unions excluded women → KOL (1869) only major union to welcome women → 400,000+ Civil War widows with no financial safety net.
p3: No minimum wage, no maternity rights, no equal pay legislation → women could not own property or sign contracts independently under coverture.

front: What was the significance of Susan B. Anthony?
p1: NWSA (1869): founded with Stanton → demanded federal constitutional amendment for women's suffrage → broader women's rights: property, divorce, employment
p2: Attempted to vote (1872): arrested in Rochester → fined $100 → refused to pay → 'I shall never pay a dollar of your unjust penalty' → national publicity for suffrage cause
p3: 15th Amendment split: NWSA refused to support 15th Amendment which gave Black men the vote but excluded women → damaged relations with abolitionists → revealed tensions within reform movement

front: What was the impact of Reconstruction on women's rights?
p1: 15th Amendment (1870): vote granted to Black men — excluded women → NWSA (Anthony/Stanton) opposed it → AWSA (Stone) supported it → split weakened suffrage movement for 20 years
p2: Anthony arrested voting in Rochester (1872) → $100 fine refused → Wyoming Territory granted female suffrage (1869) → Women's Crusade (1873): 50,000 marched → WCTU founded (1874)
p3: Black women excluded from both NWSA and AWSA → Reconstruction Congress focused entirely on African American male rights → women's suffrage treated as separate, secondary question

front: What were the Comstock Laws (1873)?
p1: Comstock Laws (1873): federal legislation making distribution of 'obscene' materials illegal → explicitly included contraceptives and information about abortion → 4,000 arrests by 1900
p2: Impact on women: reproductive decisions criminalised → wealthy women accessed contraception through private doctors → working-class and immigrant women had no access → exacerbated class inequality
p3: Resistance: early challenge by Emma Goldman and others → arrested multiple times for distributing birth control information → demonstrated state actively policed women's bodies

front: What was the significance of Frances Willard and the WCTU?
p1: WCTU (1874): Frances Willard became leader from 1879 → 'Do Everything' strategy: temperance + suffrage + social reform → largest women's organisation in the world by 1890s
p2: Political influence: lobbied for 8-hour working day, prison reform, kindergartens alongside temperance → 300,000 members by the 1890s → Willard died 1898 before seeing any amendments
p3: Divisions: temperance imposed middle-class Protestant values → alienated Catholic immigrant women and working-class women → WCTU's narrow moral focus limited coalition-building

front: What was the significance of Jane Addams and Hull House?
p1: Hull House (1889): founded in Chicago → 2,000+ people served per week by second year → social services, education, cultural programmes for poor immigrant women and families
p2: Political influence: Addams lobbied for child labour laws, 8-hour working day, workplace safety → National Consumers League connection → brought middle-class reformers into working-class communities
p3: Significance: settlement house movement linked social work to political reform → cross-class solidarity → model replicated in 400 settlement houses nationwide → BUT focused on assimilation of immigrants

front: What were working conditions like for women in the Gilded Age?
p1: Wages: women earned approximately half of male wages throughout → immigrant women: 70 hours/week for $5 → domestic service: paid $3-5/week with no protections → clerical workers slightly better
p2: Conditions: factory work — unventilated, unlit, dangerous machinery → no safety regulations → no workers' compensation for injury → owners could lock exits (as Triangle Shirtwaist would later expose)
p3: Exclusion from unions: AFL excluded most women → male unions opposed women working → Women's Trade Union League (WTUL, 1903) formed to fill gap → limited success in male-dominated movement

front: What were the gains for women during the Gilded Age?
p1: Education: 111,000 women in higher education (21%) by 1870 → 32% by 1880 → by 1900, half of all high school graduates were female → access to teaching, secretarial, nursing professions
p2: Suffrage: Wyoming (1869), Colorado (1893), Utah and Idaho (1896) granted female suffrage → 4 states by end of period → NAWSA (1890) unified movement nationally
p3: Economic: birth rate fell from 5.42 (1850) to 3.56 (1900) → reduced domestic burden → by 1900 c.1 million working women as teachers, secretaries, librarians, telephone operators

front: What were the limits on women's progress during the Gilded Age?
p1: No federal suffrage → Minor v Happersett (1875) blocked route → only 4 states by 1900 → women paid half male wages → immigrant women: 70 hours/week for $5.
p2: Education gains for white middle class only → Black women excluded from mainstream suffrage → Comstock Laws blocked reproductive rights.
p3: Temperance movement: WCTU imposed middle-class values → alienated working-class immigrant women → divided potential coalition → suffrage framed as 'moral' reform rather than political right.

front: How effective were women's movements in the Gilded Age?
p1: NWSA: Anthony attempted to vote (1872) → arrested → $100 fine refused → national attention → AWSA: state victories — Wyoming, Colorado, Utah → NAWSA (1890) unified movement
p2: National Consumer League (1899): workplace safety advocacy → YWCA (1867): helped urban women → National Association of Coloured Women (1896): Ida B. Wells fought for Black women outside mainstream.
p3: Effectiveness real but limited: women influenced government through 'moral' sphere → built powerful national organisations → BUT no federal suffrage despite 30+ years

front: How ineffective were women's movements in the Gilded Age?
p1: Union exclusion: male unions refused women's strikes → 1882 Lawrence: no union support → only 2% of trade unionists women by 1900 → AFL excluded women
p2: Class and race: middle-class white women dominated movements → working-class, immigrant and Black women excluded → temperance imposed middle-class values on working-class immigrant communities.
p3: Structural limits: no federal suffrage despite decades → Minor v Happersett (1875) blocked constitutional route

front: How united were women in the Gilded Age?
p1: United: NWSA and AWSA despite tactical differences both pushed for suffrage → unified into NAWSA (1890) → WCTU united women across class lines around temperance and moral reform
p2: Class divisions: middle-class women focused on suffrage and temperance → immigrant and working-class women worked 70 hours/week and prioritised wages → Anti-Suffrage League argued women's place was in the home
p3: Race divisions: Black women excluded from mainstream NAWSA → Ida B. Wells excluded from organisations → Black women's concerns (lynching, disenfranchisement) systematically sidelined by white leadership

front: How divided were women in the Gilded Age?
p1: Class: middle-class focused on suffrage and temperance → working-class focused on wages and labour rights → 1882 Lawrence: no suffragist support → temperance was middle-class imposition on immigrant cultures
p2: Race: Black women excluded from NAWSA → Ida B. Wells fought double oppression from outside mainstream → National Association of Coloured Women (1896) required as separate organisation
p3: Tactical: NWSA vs AWSA split over 15th Amendment — weakened campaign for 20 years → 19th Amendment secured white women's vote

front: What was the significance of Carrie Chapman Catt and NAWSA?
p1: NAWSA (1890): merger of NWSA and AWSA under Catt → 'Winning Plan' (1916): combined state campaigns with federal amendment push → 2 million members by 1919
p2: 19th Amendment (1920): NAWSA's 50-year campaign succeeded → Catt founded League of Women Voters (1920) immediately after — to educate newly-enfranchised female electorate
p3: Limits: NAWSA prioritised white Southern women's support → Black women forced to march at back of 1913 Suffrage Parade

front: What was the significance of Alice Paul?
p1: CUWS (1913): Paul and Lucy Burns → militant tactics — picketed White House, hunger strikes → 7-month prison sentence → refused to be treated as criminal → force-fed → massive publicity
p2: Silent Sentinels: daily White House pickets from 1917 → 'Kaiser Wilson' banners → arrested 168 times → publicity forced Wilson to reverse opposition to suffrage
p3: ERA (1923): Paul first introduced Equal Rights Amendment → demanded immediate legal equality not gradual reform → opposed by social feminists who feared it would remove protective labour legislation

front: What was the significance of the Triangle Shirtwaist Fire (1911)?
p1: New York City, March 1911 → fire on upper floors of Triangle Shirtwaist Factory → owners had locked exit doors
p2: 100,000 marched at victims' funeral → New York Factory Commission: comprehensive investigation led by Frances Perkins
p3: Significance: galvanised labour movement around women workers' safety → Perkins later used findings to shape New Deal legislation → showed male union neglect had lethal consequences

front: What was the significance of the Bread and Roses Strike (1912)?
p1: Lawrence, Massachusetts → mill owners cut wages after 54-hour work week law reduced hours → 20,000+ immigrant women struck — IWW-led → 51 nationalities
p2: Tactics: picketing, marches, children sent to union families in other cities — generated public sympathy → no male union support → Elizabeth Gurley Flynn central to leadership.
p3: Success: 15% pay rise, overtime pay, no discrimination against strikers → showed immigrant working-class women could win major industrial dispute through solidarity

front: What was the impact of WWI on women's rights?
p1: Employment: 40% of women employed during war → entered manufacturing, engineering, transport → proved women could perform traditionally male roles → but mostly replaced returning soldiers after war
p2: Political: WWI service strengthened suffrage argument → 'if you fight, you vote' logic → Wilson reversed opposition to suffrage → 19th Amendment passed 1919, ratified 1920
p3: Limited gains: most women returned to domestic roles after war → wages dropped → trade unions excluded women → wartime opportunity was temporary not transformative

front: What was the impact of the 19th Amendment (1920)?
p1: 19th Amendment (1920): vote granted after 50 years → BUT only 1/3 of women voted compared to 2/3 of men in 1920s → low political engagement in first decade
p2: Black women: continued to face voter suppression in South through poll taxes, literacy tests and violence → 19th Amendment theoretical for Southern Black women until Voting Rights Act decades later
p3: Political representation: women slow to enter political office → Nellie Tayloe Ross (first female governor, 1925) → League of Women Voters educated but did not transform participation levels

front: What was the significance of Margaret Sanger?
p1: Brooklyn clinic (1916): served 20,000 women → shut down for violating Comstock Laws → Sanger arrested and jailed → continued campaign from exile
p2: American Birth Control League (1921): founded to increase access to contraception → lobbied Congress to exempt birth control from obscenity laws → 222 clinics by 1930s
p3: Shepherd-Towner Act (1921): first federal maternity and infant health funding → ABCL lobbied alongside this federal initiative → BUT funding ended 1929, Comstock Laws remained → eugenics controversy undermined Sanger's legacy and universality of reproductive rights

front: What was flapper culture and what did it represent?
p1: Flapper culture: young, urban, white, middle-class women — dancing, smoking, drinking, short hair, short skirts → challenge to Victorian femininity → birth rate falling, marriage age rising
p2: BUT: limited to white urban middle class → rural, working-class, Black and immigrant women unaffected or hostile
p3: 80% of Americans in 1936 Gallup poll: married women should not take men's jobs → Comstock Laws still in force

front: What was the significance of Frances Perkins and Eleanor Roosevelt?
p1: Frances Perkins: first female Cabinet member — Secretary of Labour 1933-45 → shaped FLSA (1938): minimum wage, 44-hour week, child labour ban → shaped Social Security Act (1935).
p2: Eleanor Roosevelt: transformed First Lady role → press conferences, newspaper column → pushed FDR on appointments → resigned from DAR to support Marian Anderson (1939).
p3: BUT: 80% in 1936 Gallup poll opposed married women working → CCC excluded women → Social Security excluded domestic and agricultural workers — majority of women of colour.

front: What were the limitations of the New Deal for women?
p1: FLSA (1938): female teachers earned 20% less than male in 1939 → CCC excluded women entirely → WPA: one-family-member policy favoured men → Social Security excluded domestic and agricultural workers.
p2: 80% in 1936 Gallup poll opposed married women working → Aid to Dependent Children reinforced motherhood role → New Deal assumed male breadwinner throughout.
p3: Black women excluded by white-administered Southern relief → Mexican American women vulnerable to deportation → rural women had least access to all programmes.

front: What were the strengths of women's position by 1932?
p1: Vote secured: 19th Amendment (1920) after 50 years → League of Women Voters educated voters → women 44% of undergraduates by 1930 → ERA introduced (1923)
p2: Growing organisations: American Birth Control League → 222 clinics by 1941 → WTUL advocating for working women → flapper culture — cultural loosening in urban middle class
p3: Political presence: some women in state legislatures and Congress → Women's Bureau (1920) in Department of Labor → League of Women Voters active

front: What were the weaknesses of women's position by 1932?
p1: Suffrage limited: only 1/3 voted in 1920s → Black women faced voter suppression in South → ERA rejected repeatedly → women earned half male wages
p2: Depression (1929): women first targeted for job losses → 80% of Americans in 1936 Gallup poll opposed married women working → Comstock Laws still in force
p3: Structural inequality unchanged: gender pay gap entrenched → professional barriers to law, medicine, business remained strong → cultural pressure for domestic sphere intensified by Depression

front: How did the New Deal improve women's position?
p1: Perkins: first female Cabinet member → FLSA (1938): minimum wage, 44-hour week, child labour ban → WPA employed 400,000 women by 1938
p2: Eleanor Roosevelt: pushed FDR on appointments → Florence Allen: first female Circuit Court judge → Bethune: led NYA Negro Affairs
p3: New Deal created legal framework supporting later equal pay campaigns → NLRB, FLSA, Social Security established precedent → BUT gender pay gap and women's structural vulnerability fundamentally unchanged.

front: What was universal about women's experience during the New Deal?
p1: All women faced 80% public opposition to married women working (1936 Gallup) → all excluded from higher-paying jobs or political decision-making → Depression devastated all women
p2: WPA employed women across racial lines — though segregated → Aid to Dependent Children reached single mothers across races — though unequally
p3: CCC excluded all women → gender pay gap universal — whether white professional or Black domestic worker → all women seen as secondary earners throughout New Deal.

front: How different were women's experiences during the New Deal?
p1: By race: Black women excluded from most relief programmes → domestic and agricultural excluded from Social Security → Mexican American women excluded from protections, vulnerable to deportation → Native American women excluded from mainstream networks.
p2: By class: middle-class accessed professional roles — Perkins, Roosevelt, Allen → working-class concentrated in excluded sectors → WPA employed women in gender-segregated lower-paid roles.
p3: By location: rural women — regardless of race — had least access → urban women accessed WPA and CIO unions → Southern women most affected by local white administrators' discrimination.

front: What was the impact of WWII on women's employment?
p1: 6 million women entered workforce during WWII → by 1944: 1 in 4 married women working → Rosie the Riveter → Lanham Act (1941): federal childcare funding for working mothers.
p2: 75% wanted to remain employed after WWII — distinct from post-WWI → entered industrial, professional and technical roles previously closed.
p3: BUT: 2 million lost jobs in 1946 as men returned → GI Bill: primarily benefited male veterans → women's undergraduate share: 40% (1920) → 30% (1950).

front: What was the significance of Dr Spock and the post-war housewife ideal?
p1: Dr Spock's Baby and Child Care (1946): 23 million copies → argued women should embrace nurturing role exclusively → reinforced 1950s suburban housewife as dominant cultural ideal.
p2: Cold War conformity: domestic sphere as women's patriotic duty → GI Bill reinforced male breadwinner → women's undergraduate share: 40% (1920) → 30% (1950).
p3: Pill approved FDA (1960) → 6 million using it by 1965 → began undermining domestic ideal → Feminine Mystique (1963) named what Dr Spock had helped create.

front: What was the Kennedy Commission on the Status of Women (1961)?
p1: Kennedy Commission (1961): Eleanor Roosevelt chaired → first federal body to document systematic sex discrimination
p2: Led directly to: Equal Pay Act (1963) — first federal legislation prohibiting pay discrimination by sex → women earning 59¢ per $1 in 1963
p3: Significance: first time federal government formally acknowledged and documented gender discrimination → broke from assumption that women's inequality was natural or acceptable → set legislative agenda for next decade

front: What were the key ideas of the Feminine Mystique (1963)?
p1: Friedan identified 'the problem with no name' → college-educated suburban housewives' profound unhappiness in prescribed domestic role → described marriage as a 'comfortable concentration camp'
p2: Argument: post-war society trapped women in domesticity → constructed by advertisers, Freudian psychologists and women's magazines → kept women out of public life and consuming domestic products
p3: Impact: 3 million copies in 3 years → Friedan co-founded NOW (1966) → launched second-wave feminism

front: What was the significance of Betty Friedan and NOW?
p1: NOW (1966): founded by Friedan → Miss America protest (1968): crowned a pig, symbolically rejected objectification → Women's Strike for Equality (1970): 50,000 marched in New York
p2: Lobbied for: Equal Pay Act (1963), Title VII enforcement, Title IX (1972), ERA ratification and reproductive rights
p3: Growing momentum: Women's Strike for Equality (1970): 50,000+ marched in New York demanding equal pay, childcare, abortion rights → National Women's Political Caucus (1971): organised women's political power → by 1972, NOW had 40,000 members — mainstream feminist organisation exerting real political pressure

front: What was the significance of the Civil Rights Act (1964) Title VII?
p1: Civil Rights Act (1964) Title VII: prohibited employment discrimination by sex → Alice Paul had lobbied for sex to be included → late addition but became one of most powerful legal tools.
p2: EEOC established to enforce → initial resistance: chairman called sex provision a 'fluke' → NOW (1966) formed partly to pressure EEOC to take sex discrimination seriously.
p3: Impact: opened professional roles to women → women could sue employers → combined with Equal Pay Act (1963): foundation for economic equality claims.

front: What was the significance of second-wave and radical feminism?
p1: Second-wave feminism: beyond suffrage → demanded economic, social and cultural equality → NOW (1966), Women's Strike for Equality (1970), Ms Magazine (1972)
p2: Radical feminism: Miss America protest (1968) — crowned a pig → Burial of True Womanhood at Arlington National Cemetery (1968) → 'The Feminists': called for abolition of marriage
p3: Tensions: radical feminism energised movement but also alienated moderates → sparked conservative backlash → Schlafly's Stop ERA mobilised around fear of radical feminism's implications

front: What was the significance of the Pill (1960)?
p1: Pill approved FDA (1960): 6 million women using it by 1965 → unprecedented autonomy over reproduction → birth rate declined sharply → enabled women to plan careers alongside family
p2: Cultural impact: separated sex from reproduction → contributed to sexual revolution → challenged traditional gender roles → gave women power over life planning previously impossible
p3: Limits: not available to unmarried women until Eisenstadt v Baird (1972) → access unequal across class and race → Catholic Church opposition → not a universal solution

front: What were Griswold v Connecticut (1965) and Eisenstadt v Baird (1972)?
p1: Griswold v Connecticut (1965): Supreme Court struck down state ban on contraceptives for married couples → right to marital privacy
p2: Eisenstadt v Baird (1972): extended contraceptive rights to unmarried individuals → built on Griswold → completed right to contraception regardless of marital status
p3: Significance: both decisions built on legal foundation Sanger had fought for since 1916 → overturned 90 years of Comstock Laws' reproductive suppression

front: What was the significance of Title IX (1972)?
p1: Title IX (1972): prohibited gender discrimination in federally funded education → universities had to provide equal opportunities in sports, academics and admissions
p2: Sports impact: women's college sports teams increased from 16,000 (1972) to 50,000 by 1978 → female athletic scholarships created → transformed women's participation in sport
p3: Limits: enforced inconsistently → many institutions slow to comply → excluded private institutions → did not address pay inequality in teaching → later threatened by Reagan budget cuts

front: What was the significance of Roe v Wade (1973)?
p1: Roe v Wade (1973): Supreme Court ruled right to abortion protected under constitutional right to privacy established in Griswold (1965) → invalidated most state abortion laws
p2: Context: National Organisation for Repeal of Abortion Laws (1969) had built pressure → combined with Griswold (1965) and Eisenstadt (1972): complete reproductive rights framework established in less than a decade.
p3: BUT: immediately polarising → National Right to Life Committee formed same year → Hyde Amendment (1976): federal abortion funding restricted — low-income women most affected

front: What was the significance of WTUL and women in the labour movement?
p1: WTUL (1903): first sustained effort to organise women workers → Bread and Roses Strike (1912): 20,000 immigrant women in Lawrence won 15% pay rise → model of cross-ethnic solidarity
p2: Triangle Shirtwaist (1911): 146 killed → Frances Perkins present → galvanised support for workplace safety → led to 36 labour laws in New York → transformed public attitude to women workers
p3: Limits: AFL consistently excluded women from skilled unions → women concentrated in non-unionised clerical and domestic work → FLSA (1938) excluded domestic workers → progress slow and contested

front: How did Black Power advance Black women's position?
p1: Triple oppression: race, gender and class intersection named → foundational for Black feminism → Elaine Brown: Chairperson of Black Panther Party → Kathleen Cleaver: BPP spokesperson
p2: Cultural reclamation: Afro hairstyle → rejected Eurocentric beauty standards → Angela Davis, Ella Baker: widely recognised → women raised profile of healthcare, education and economic opportunity as Black women's concerns.
p3: Community work: women central to survival programmes — day care, food, health → demonstrated Black women could lead own struggles → Black feminism emerged as distinct intellectual and political movement.

front: How did Black Power limit the position of Black women?
p1: Male chauvinism in BPP: women relegated to typing, cooking, logistics → ideas ignored unless proposed by men (Cleaver) → 'revolutionary first, Sister second'
p2: NOI: rejected birth control → criticised women challenging traditional gender roles → Black Power leaders viewed feminism as 'white women's issue' → focus on reclaiming Black masculinity limited gender equality.
p3: NOW focused on white middle-class concerns → Black women's triple oppression only slowly incorporated → white feminists rarely engaged with racial justice

front: How did Black Power influence the wider women's movement?
p1: Intersectionality: Black Power highlighted race, gender and class intersections → foundational for Black feminism and mainstream feminist theory → militant tactics: radical feminism adopted direct-action approaches inspired by Black Panthers.
p2: NOW pushed — slowly — to incorporate racial justice → Angela Davis, Elaine Brown, Kathleen Cleaver brought revolutionary spirit to feminism → Fannie Lou Hamer demonstrated Black women could lead own struggles.
p3: Tactical influence: fish-ins, occupations and confrontational media strategies all influenced by Black Power → second-wave feminism more militant because of Black Power's example.

front: How limited was Black Power's influence on the women's movement?
p1: NOW and mainstream feminists continued to focus on white middle-class concerns — equal pay, reproductive rights — often sidelining the unique struggles of Black women
p2: Black Power leaders dismissed feminism as 'a white movement' — focus on reclaiming Black masculinity limited full integration of women's concerns into Black Power agenda
p3: Radical feminism's rise was driven by multiple factors: Betty Friedan, the pill, and second-wave feminism were equally significant — Black Power was one influence among several

front: What was the significance of Phyllis Schlafly and Stop ERA?
p1: Stop ERA (1972): Schlafly launched immediately after ERA passed Congress → argued ERA would eliminate protective legislation, force women into combat, require unisex bathrooms, destroy traditional family
p2: Tactics: mobilised conservative and working-class women → evangelical Christian women's organisations provided grassroots base → by 1982 only 35 of 38 states ratified → ERA dead
p3: Significance: showed conservative women's political mobilisation could match progressive women's → Schlafly herself a lawyer — used freedoms feminism had created to campaign against further feminist gains

front: What was the political polarisation over abortion after Roe v Wade?
p1: Before Roe: abortion not a major partisan issue → both parties contained pro-choice and anti-abortion politicians.
p2: After Roe: National Right to Life Committee (1973) → Republican Party adopted anti-abortion platform → Reagan (1981-89): opposed abortion rights, made conservative Supreme Court appointments.
p3: By 1992: abortion primary gender issue splitting parties → Planned Parenthood v Casey (1992): Supreme Court allowed state restrictions → showed ongoing vulnerability of Roe.

front: What was the ERA and why did it fail?
p1: ERA: first proposed by Alice Paul (1923) → reintroduced every Congress for 50 years → passed Congress (1972): constitutional guarantee equal rights could not be denied on account of sex
p2: Schlafly's Stop ERA: argued ERA would eliminate protective legislation, force women into combat, destroy traditional family → mobilised conservative and religious women
p3: Significance: by 1992 no constitutional guarantee of sex equality in the USA → every legislative gain — Equal Pay Act, Title VII, Title IX — remained vulnerable

front: What was the anti-feminist backlash of the 1970s–80s?
p1: Moral Majority (1979): Falwell's evangelical coalition opposed abortion, ERA and feminism. National Right to Life Committee (1973): formed in direct response to Roe. Phyllis Schlafly's Stop ERA framed feminism as threat to traditional family
p2: Reagan: cuts to welfare, childcare and reproductive health harmed women. Hyde Amendment (1976): restricted federal abortion funding → class dimension to reproductive rights
p3: BUT backlash did not reverse all gains → Sandra Day O'Connor: first female Supreme Court Justice (1981). Sally Ride (1983). Geraldine Ferraro: first woman VP nominee (1984). 60% of women employed by 1992

front: What were the political rights of women by 1992?
p1: Year of the Woman: 24 women elected to House (11%), 6 to Senate → O'Connor: first female Supreme Court Justice (1981) → Ferraro: first female VP nominee (1984).
p2: 55% women voted vs 49% men → political participation exceeded men's → BUT ERA unratified — no constitutional guarantee of sex equality → Roe under threat from Casey (1992).
p3: Women's Political Caucus (1971) had built pipeline → BUT only 10% of elected federal officials were women → glass ceiling in politics as well as workplace.

front: What was the social position of women by 1992?
p1: 60% of women employed — working mothers the norm → average 2.2 children — lowest since 19th century → women outpacing men in graduation: 84% vs 78%.
p2: 40% of law and medical degrees → Title IX (1972) transformed girls' sports and education → BUT domestic violence still underreported and underprosecuted → rape shield laws still developing.
p3: Roe v Wade (1973) gave reproductive rights → BUT Hyde Amendment (1976) restricted funding → Planned Parenthood v Casey (1992) allowed state restrictions → rights fragile.

front: What was the economic position of women by 1992?
p1: Women 40% of workforce → 75¢ per $1 (up from 59¢ in 1963) → glass ceiling: only 10% of senior management were women.
p2: Equal Pay Act (1963) + Title VII (1964) gave legal foundation → EEOC enforced → BUT enforcement slow and glass ceiling entrenched → CLUW (1974) pushed unions on equal pay.
p3: Deindustrialisation hit women in manufacturing → but service sector growth created new employment → women dominated healthcare, education, retail — often lower-paid sectors.
